yaml.title: Phenological Changes in Pollination Pals
yaml.author: Aubrey Monaco
yaml.subtitle: Synchrony Shifts in the Ruby-Throated Hummingbird and Preferred Flowers

markdown.markdown:
With warming temperatures due to anthropogenic climate change, migrating birds are tending to move back to their breeding grounds earlier each year [1]. Along with this, flowers that certain migrating birds, like Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (Archilochus colubris), feed on may be changing the time of their first bloom due to climate change [2].

![[Ruby-throated Hummingbird [3]]{style="color:darkblue;"}](data/rth_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="400"}

I want to investigate how the Ruby-throated Hummingbird has been shifting its spring migration patterns, and how the appearances of two spring ephemeral species it prefers to feed on during this migration, Red Buckeye (Aesculus pavia) and Red Columbine (Aquilegia canadensis), has changed (or not changed) over the past 10* years [4].

*My maps and graphs are from 2014 to 2025 to account for any incomplete datasets from 2025

![[Red Columbine [5]]{style="color:darkred;"}](data/cb_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="200"}

![[Red Buckeye [6]]{style="color:darkred;"}](data/rb_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="226"}

I predict that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are migrating back to their breeding grounds earlier each year, and that they are arriving at higher latitudes increasingly earlier than lower latitudes. Additionally, I suppose that the first sightings of these preferred flowers will be earlier at higher latitudes and later at lower latitudes compared to previous years. So, as Ruby-throated Hummingbirds migrate back earlier, these flowers may not be available at lower latitudes for them to feed on.

## 5. Flowers: Calculate Means of Early Period (2005-2013)

- Found the mean date of first flower sightings from 2005 to 2013 and from March to May (when these flowers' bloom times overlap) [7,8]

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

  filter(latitude > 30 & latitude < 33) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

fl_early_33 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 33 & latitude < 36) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

fl_early_36 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 36 & latitude < 39) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

fl_early_39 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 39 & latitude < 42) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

fl_early_42 <- fl_early %>%

fl_early_45 <- fl_early %>%
  filter(latitude > 45 & latitude < 48) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE))

fl_early_all <- rbind(fl_early_30, fl_early_33, fl_early_36, fl_early_39, fl_early_42, fl_early_45)

#Checked each dataset for the mean bloom date

```

## 6. Flowers: Calculate Means and Difference From 2014-2025 to 2005-2013

- Added a column (mean0013) with the means of the fl_early observations based on latitude
- Used 6 bands of latitude for more specific analysis
- Created a "difference" column, showing the difference in days of arrival between the early and current average using mean - mean0013
- Rejoined all of these bands into one dataset for plotting

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
fl_new <- all_flower %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025) & month %in% c(3, 4, 5)) %>%
  mutate(mean0013 = 
         case_when(
         latitude > 30 & latitude < 33 ~ 82.06329,
         latitude > 33 & latitude < 36 ~ 103,
         latitude > 36 & latitude < 39 ~ 120.5417,
         latitude > 39 & latitude < 42 ~ 125.6289,
         latitude > 42 & latitude < 45 ~ 132.7564,
         latitude > 45 & latitude < 48 ~ 140.3333))

fl_30 <- fl_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 30 & latitude < 33) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_33 <- fl_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 33 & latitude < 36) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_36 <- fl_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 36 & latitude < 39) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_39 <- fl_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 39 & latitude < 42) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_42 <- fl_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 42 & latitude < 45) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_45 <- fl_new %>%
  filter(latitude > 45 & latitude < 48) %>%
  mutate(mean = mean(year_day, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(difference = mean - mean0013)

fl_new_all <- rbind(fl_30, fl_33, fl_36, fl_39, fl_42, fl_45)

```

    ) %>%

Dates for each latitude band:

-   30-33: March 31st (About 8 days later)

-   33-36: April 12th (About 1 day earlier)

Trends for Red Columbine and Red Buckeye show that the timing of first observations have somewhat changed from the 2005-2013 average. At the highest latitudes, there is not much change in flowering times. But for latitudes between 30 and 36, flowers have been sighted both earlier and later than in previous years. Since these flowers are spring ephemerals, warmer winter temperatures, or more extreme heat in spring and summer, may cause this trend, as these flowers will not bloom under extreme heat, or until they have gone through a period of sufficient cooling [10].

Additionally, the average first observation date for Ruby-throated hummingbirds has been generally shifting earlier with increasing latitudes.

These trends do somewhat align, especially at higher latitudes. So, these food sources will be available when Ruby-throats migrate back to higher latitudes earlier. But, Ruby-throats may may miss the flowering of these plants at lower latitudes.

It is important to note that this dataset is relatively small, and data used to acquire average arrival/bloom dates for 2005 to 2013 was sparse. # Introduction

With warming temperatures due to anthropogenic climate change, migrating birds are tending to move back to their breeding grounds earlier each year [1]. Along with this, flowers that certain migrating birds, like Ruby-throated Hummingbirds (Archilochus colubris), feed on may be changing the time of their first bloom due to climate change [2].

![[Ruby-throated Hummingbird [3]]{style="color:darkblue;"}](data/rth_1.jpg){fig-align="center" width="400"}

I want to investigate how the Ruby-throated Hummingbird has been shifting its spring migration patterns, and how the appearances of two spring ephemeral species it prefers to feed on during this migration, Red Buckeye (Aesculus pavia) and Red Columbine (Aquilegia canadensis), has changed (or not changed) over the past 10* years [4].

*My maps and graphs are from 2014 to 2025 to account for any incomplete datasets from 2025

I predict that Ruby-throated Hummingbirds are migrating back to their breeding grounds earlier each year, and that they are arriving at higher latitudes increasingly earlier than lower latitudes. Additionally, I suppose that the first sightings of these preferred flowers will be earlier at higher latitudes and later at lower latitudes compared to previous years. # Conclusions

Trends for Red Columbine and Red Buckeye show that the timing of first observations have somewhat changed from the 2005-2013 average. At the highest latitudes, there is not much change in flowering times. But for latitudes between 30 and 36, flowers have been sighted both earlier and later than in previous years. Since these flowers are spring ephemerals, warmer winter temperatures, or more extreme heat in spring and summer, may cause this trend, as these flowers will not bloom under extreme heat, or until they have gone through a period of sufficient cooling [10].

Additionally, the average first observation date for Ruby-throated hummingbirds has been generally shifting earlier with increasing latitudes.

These trends do somewhat align, especially at higher latitudes. So, these food sources will be available when Ruby-throats migrate back to higher latitudes earlier. But, Ruby-throats may may miss the flowering of these plants at lower latitudes.

It is important to note that this dataset is relatively small, and data used to acquire average arrival/bloom dates for 2005 to 2013 was sparse. Additionally, since this data is collected from citizen science projects, the data may be more biased towards urban areas, and its distribution is not even. As shown in the heatmap for the flowers, observations do tend to be concentrated in urban areas.
